transcript.text: Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-38
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A monopolist compares marginal revenue with marginal cost to choose output, then reads the corresponding price from demand. In the displayed interior solution, MR exceeds MC before their crossing and falls below MC afterward. The output decision and the price decision are separate; marginal cost need not always slope upward.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the output where MR crosses MC from above in the interior solution.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.
Keep the output decision and price decision separate: marginal conditions determine quantity, demand determines price.
Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MONOPOLY PRICE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down from price 60 at quantity 0 to zero at 120. MR slopes down more steeply, reaching zero at 60. At quantity 40, MR and rising MC meet at 20; demand is at 40 and ATC at 45, with dashed guides. Demand and MC intersect near quantity 67 and price 27. ATC is U-shaped, reaching its minimum to the right of quantity 40. The 67 and 27 intersection values are approximate as labeled.

The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.
CHECK YOURSELF
What is the correct order for solving a monopoly graph?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-40
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Compared with competition, monopoly usually restricts output, raises price, transfers surplus, and creates deadweight loss. Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not. The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare monopoly output and price with the competitive benchmark where price equals marginal cost.
Monopoly normally produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
Separate the transfer of surplus to the monopolist from surplus lost through reduced output.
Deadweight loss is the value of trades between monopoly output and the efficient quantity that no longer occur.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to reverse monopoly competitive comparison. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING MONOPOLY DEADWEIGHT LOSS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down, and MR slopes down more steeply from the same vertical intercept. MC is horizontal at 20. MR meets MC near quantity 45; at that quantity, guides mark demand price about 47 and ATC about 24. Demand meets MC at quantity 90 and price 20; ATC there is slightly above 20. ATC declines throughout the displayed relevant range. The marked demand price at 45 is approximately 47.

The unregulated monopoly chooses about 45 units where MR = MC and charges the demand price of about $47. The efficient outcome occurs where demand meets MC: 90 units at $20. Monopoly therefore restricts output and raises price, leaving mutually beneficial units between 45 and 90 unproduced.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Price Discrimination
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-42
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Price Discrimination.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price discrimination charges different buyers different prices for the same product when resale can be prevented. Preventing resale is what allows separated prices to persist. Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable. Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
Price discrimination requires control over price and a way to distinguish relevant buyers or markets.
Perfect discrimination can expand output to the efficient quantity while transferring surplus to the seller.
The firm allocates output across separated markets using marginal revenue relative to marginal cost.
Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to disconnect wtp from first degree efficiency. Charging each unit up to willingness to pay can make serving all units with value at least MC profitable.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING PRICE DISCRIMINATION

A theater charges students $8 and other adults $14 for the same seat. The policy can persist only if students cannot resell discounted tickets to adults; otherwise arbitrage would erase the price difference. Verification separates the groups, and the different prices reflect different demand elasticities.
CHECK YOURSELF
A seller charges students less than other buyers. Why must it be able to identify the groups and prevent resale for this pricing policy to persist?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-44
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
WATCH OUT
Separate profit from shutdown. A fixed-cost increase can create an economic loss without changing marginal cost or the benefit of operating; compare revenue with variable cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN FIRM DECISION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The displayed baseline has Q = 36 and P = ATC = $27, so economic profit is zero. Consider a higher fixed lease cost of $108, with demand and variable costs unchanged. Output and price stay at that baseline, but ATC rises by $3 and the loss is $108. The firm still operates if revenue covers variable cost; loss alone does not imply shutdown.
CHECK YOURSELF
A firm earns a loss because P is below ATC. What additional cost comparison is needed to decide whether it should shut down in the short run?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-45
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

Short-run profit attracts competing varieties, reducing demand for each incumbent. Adjustment continues until demand is tangent to ATC at the chosen output. The graph shows that endpoint at 36 units and $27, where revenue and cost both equal $972. Tangency eliminates economic profit; it does not put output at minimum ATC.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does excess capacity measure?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-46
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Advertising, Branding & Nonprice Competition.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Advertising can give buyers product information, persuade them, or build a brand. Information about prices, hours, or features can reduce search costs. Persuasive messages can change preferences or price sensitivity. Nonprice competition also includes quality, convenience, service, and variety.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A shoe company introduces custom colors and faster delivery while leaving its posted price unchanged.
Consumers cannot directly observe product durability before purchase.
A firm buys a one-time advertising campaign that does not change demand.
A perfume ad links the brand with status and excitement but provides almost no factual product information.
A branding campaign leaves the number of buyers unchanged but makes them less price sensitive.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat every advertisement as useful information or as waste. Ask what it tells buyers and whether it changes their ability to compare products.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INFORMATIVE OR PERSUASIVE ADVERTISING?

A pharmacy advertises that a prescription costs $8 and that it stays open until 10 p.m. Buyers can compare stores more easily, so search costs fall; this is informational advertising. A separate campaign associates the brand with status without adding product facts; that campaign is persuasive advertising. Both compete without directly cutting price.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does nonprice competition mean?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

Variety may create utility even while markup and excess capacity remain.
Variety can create utility even with efficiency costs.
Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.
Two markets have the same total production cost.

A common mistake is to misapply monopolistic competition rule. Differentiation can create consumer value through variety even when the standard model shows some productive inefficiency.

Two bakeries offer different breads. A neighborhood values having both varieties, but dividing sales between the bakeries can leave each producing below its lowest-cost scale. Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-50
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Collusion, Cartels & Prisoner's-Dilemma Incentives.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.
The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.
A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
Three firms agree to keep prices high.
WATCH OUT
Do not miss individual incentive to defect. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.
WORKED EXAMPLE: INDIVIDUAL INCENTIVES VERSUS JOINT GAINS

If Column keeps the agreement, Row gets 8 by undercutting rather than 6 by keeping it. If Column undercuts, Row gets 3 rather than 2 by undercutting. Column faces the same incentives. Both undercut and receive 3 each, although keeping the agreement would give 6 each. Individual incentives can undermine a mutually beneficial agreement.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the other firm keeps the agreement, why is a one-time promise to keep it vulnerable to undercutting?

Factor Markets & Labor Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-57
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal productivity to analyze labor demand, wages, and employment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor demand is derived from the value workers add to output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker. For a price-taking seller, VMP = output price x MPL. A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where VMP equals the wage.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A wage change causes movement along labor demand; productivity or output-price changes shift labor demand.
Higher product demand, output price, or worker productivity shifts labor demand right.
Worker preferences, population, migration, training, and alternative jobs can shift labor supply.
Competitive wage and employment occur where market labor demand intersects market labor supply.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse MPL with VMP. MPL is extra physical output; VMP converts that output into dollars by multiplying by the output price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPETITIVE LABOR-MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Horizontal axis: hundreds of warehouse workers; vertical axis: hourly wage in dollars. Labor Demand slopes down from wage 30 at quantity 0 to zero at 120 hundreds. Labor Supply slopes up from wage 10. They intersect at wage 20 and quantity 40 hundreds of workers, with dashed guides to both axes. Supply lies above demand to the right of that intersection.

Suppose output sells for $5 and the marginal worker adds 4 units per hour. VMP is $5 x 4 = $20 per hour, matching a $20 wage. The graph shows market equilibrium at that wage and 40 hundreds of workers, or 4,000 workers. A higher output price raises VMP at each employment level and shifts labor demand right.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the output price rises while worker productivity is unchanged, what happens to labor demand?

Consumer Choice
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-58
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows affordable bundles at given income and prices. Its intercepts show the most of either good a consumer can buy. An indifference curve connects bundles the consumer ranks equally. The best affordable bundle reaches the highest available preference level; in this example, its curve just touches the budget line.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
Compare the highest preference curve that can be reached without exceeding the budget.
WATCH OUT
Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BEST AFFORDABLE BUNDLE

Horizontal axis: Good X; vertical axis: Good Y. A straight budget line runs from 40 units of Y at X = 0 to 20 units of X at Y = 0. Marked bundle A is X = 10 and Y = 20. At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.
CHECK YOURSELF
If only the price of Y falls, does the budget line shift in parallel or pivot?

Condorcet Paradox & Voting Cycles
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-66
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain how pairwise majority rule can generate cyclic collective preferences.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Even when every voter has a consistent ranking, pairwise majority voting can produce a cycle: A defeats B, B defeats C, and C defeats A. The group then has no option that defeats every alternative, and agenda order can affect the final outcome.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
There are at least three alternatives and voters rank them differently.
Compare alternatives two at a time using majority rule.
The collective relation cycles even though each individual's ranking is consistent.
Because no option is a universal majority winner, agenda order may matter.
WATCH OUT
A voting cycle does not require irrational voters. Individually transitive rankings can aggregate into an intransitive majority relation.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THREE VOTERS, THREE OPTIONS

Using the rankings, A defeats B by 2 votes to 1; B defeats C by 2 to 1; and C defeats A by 2 to 1. Each voter has a consistent ranking, yet the group cycles. With no option beating every rival, the order of pairwise votes can affect the final survivor.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can changing the order of pairwise votes change the winner when majority preferences form a cycle?

Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-67
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain the basic limitation on combining individual rankings into a social ranking.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

With at least three alternatives, Arrow's theorem shows that no ranked-choice social decision rule can guarantee all of a specified set of desirable conditions at once. The result identifies a tradeoff among aggregation properties; it does not prove that democracy or every voting system is impossible.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
The problem combines individual rankings into a complete and consistent social ranking.
Desirable conditions include respecting unanimity and avoiding control by one dictator.
Independence of irrelevant alternatives limits how an outside option may change a pairwise ranking.
The theorem concerns simultaneous guarantees under its conditions, not whether voting can occur.
WATCH OUT
Do not conclude that no voting system works or that democracy is impossible. The theorem applies to ranked aggregation and the simultaneous satisfaction of specified conditions.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DESIRABLE RULES IN TENSION

A community wants all five guarantees in the table. With at least three alternatives, Arrow's theorem says no rule combining unrestricted individual rankings can always provide every guarantee. The introductory lesson is a design tradeoff among reasonable goals, not that elections cannot produce winners.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which is accurate: Arrow identifies incompatible guarantees under stated conditions, or proves that no election can produce a winner?

Median Voter Theorem
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-68
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain why majority-rule competition can favor the median voter's position under specific assumptions.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

When policy lies on one dimension, preferences are single-peaked, and decisions use majority rule, the median voter's preferred position has a special advantage. Policies or candidates may move toward it because alternatives on either side can be defeated by a majority.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Place voters along one policy dimension and identify the middle preferred position.
Each voter has a single peak and prefers positions less as they move away from it.
Pairwise decisions use majority rule.
Competition can favor the median, but the conclusion depends on these assumptions.
WATCH OUT
The median voter does not always decide elections. Multidimensional policy, non-single-peaked preferences, turnout, institutions, or other departures can break the result.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THE PIVOTAL POLICY POSITION

One policy axis marks ideal points 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. Median is 30. Voters at 10, 20 and 30 form a majority for 30 against a higher proposal. Voters at 30, 40 and 50 form a majority for 30 against a lower proposal. The example assumes single-peaked preferences and pairwise majority rule.

Five voters prefer policy levels 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. The ordered middle preference is 30. Against a proposal below 30, the voters at 30, 40, and 50 form a majority for 30; against one above 30, the voters at 10, 20, and 30 form a majority for 30. Under one-dimensional, single-peaked preferences and majority rule, the median position can defeat alternatives on either side.
CHECK YOURSELF
For preferred policies 5, 15, 25, 35, and 45, which position is median, and what preference assumption is required?

Pairwise decisions use majority rule.
Competition can favor the median, but the conclusion depends on these assumptions.
WATCH OUT
The median voter does not always decide elections. Multidimensional policy, non-single-peaked preferences, turnout, institutions, or other departures can break the result.
WORKED EXAMPLE: THE PIVOTAL POLICY POSITION

One policy axis marks ideal points 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. Median is 30. Voters at 10, 20 and 30 form a majority for 30 against a higher proposal. Voters at 30, 40 and 50 form a majority for 30 against a lower proposal. The example assumes single-peaked preferences and pairwise majority rule.

Five voters prefer policy levels 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50. The ordered middle preference is 30. Against a proposal below 30, the voters at 30, 40, and 50 form a majority for 30; against one above 30, the voters at 10, 20, and 30 form a majority for 30. Under one-dimensional, single-peaked preferences and majority rule, the median position can defeat alternatives on either side.
